Addressing matrix multiplication—a fundamental and widely utilized operation in computing—this paper begins by detailing the formula and logical rationale behind the algorithm. Furthermore, the study presents a side-by-side comparison of sequential and GPU-based parallel execution algorithms regarding both correctness and performance. Using Python for implementation and benchmarks, the research examines comprehensive tables that contrast execution times, the number of employed instructions, and specific performance metrics, ultimately validating the anticipated efficiency gains of the parallel approach.

This paper outlines the development of a new, effective, and practical strategy solving a real-world challenge: multi-agent collaboration in task assignment and decision-making. This approach integrates a unique, high-level decision-making architecture designed to significantly improve current methodologies. Key features include (1) limiting the number of decision variables in each step, (2) minimizing discrete continuous optimization operations, and (3) reducing dependency on extensive parameter tuning. Consequently, even with basic communication and computational tools, a significant increase in decision efficiency is observed. Notably, compared to recent state-of-the-art algorithms, our method cuts calculation loads by approximately 90%. Despite these constraints, when applied to a dual-robot crate carrying scenario, simulations revealed that our algorithm delivers comparable or superior outcomes.

When evaluating scattering amplitudes at high orders in perturbative quantum field theory, multiple soft virtual contributions typically give rise to infrared (IR) divergences. Allowing amplitude calculations to reach sufficiently high loops enables the resummation of these virtual factors, rendering their exact value unnecessary; meanwhile, the resulting infinity mirrors that of real IR pairs, suggesting a parallel approach. This paper explores amplitude-based resummation methods, focusing in particular on IR-resummation techniques applied specifically within-resummation frameworks. Such methods have already proven their mettle in advanced AM-Evaluation tasks extending to nearly loop order, achieving percent-level accuracy in specific observables like the Higgs boson production cross. We introduce for the first time in amplitude-based calculations a novel framework combining runtime amplitude evaluation with external loop corrections. Applying to gluon fusion reactions extending to loop orders reveals a surprising result regarding the residual divergences. We observe that remaining infinities originate not merely from infrared sources but also substantially from ultraviolet contributions. We further note that even after subtracting standard divergences a small but non-negligible finite remainder persists. Its structure is found to share remarkable similarities with missing finite terms at the leading order of the conventional theory. We also identify significant challenges associated specifically implementing this approach within-amplitude calculations, which we hope future work will address.

In the vertical federated learning framework applicable to education, schools collaborate to construct unified models while maintaining the secrecy of individual data points. Yet, these collaborative schemes are vulnerable to specific privacy attacks: practitioners may infer sensitive attributes by analyzing parameter update patterns across multiple training rounds. To formalize this threat, we introduce the concept of pragmatic privacy assault by integrating update information with auxiliary knowledge sourced from outside the dataset. Our approach generates pragmatic profiles that link individuals to events occurring in the real world, wherein the associated identifiers remain implicit in updated neural network weights. Our investigation reveals that even with limited extraneous data, such attacks achieve substantial precision and recall. Furthermore, increasing the granularity of auxiliary information significantly enhances both accuracy rates. A variety of mitigation measures are also explored and tested; while some reduce overall performance, others effectively neutralize the threat.

Kernel estimation of a circular probability distribution represents a well-established technique; however, evaluating the estimator's true error demand prohibitive computational resources due to the necessity of measuring distances between data points and test samples. To overcome this limitation, we propose an accelerated and space-efficient algorithm that leverages a set of pseudo-random Fourier attributes to perform Data Dependent Kernel Estimation (DKRE) on circular distributions, which yields results equivalent in accuracy to standard DKRE but operates significantly faster. Furthermore, this adaptive algorithm dynamically determines the bandwidth based on specific data characteristics, similar to enhanced histogram methods for linear distributions, while extensive simulations validate the approach's efficacy.

Deep learning techniques are increasingly applied in cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) analysis to automate image segmentation, although most models are developed using datasets from healthy adults and may fail to generalize for children suffering from congenital heart disease (CHD). This study evaluated the cross-species translation of three voxel-wise UNet-based automatic segmentation tools—designed specifically for CMR myocardial characterization—when applied to pediatric CHD cases. We analyzed data from 10 children (ages 4 to 16) diagnosed with various CHD types, capturing segmentations prior to and following interventions between 2015 and 2020. The direct application of these algorithms to these pediatric datasets without retraining or fine-tuning yielded poor, inconsistent segmentations. However, the failure to generalize was successfully resolved by training the networks on a smaller dataset derived specifically from the same pediatric population, or by utilizing transfer learning. With both strategies, all three algorithms produced high-performance, robust automatic segmentations. These findings indicate that current UNet architectures are flexible and can be efficiently adapted to accommodate pediatric CHD morphology through the use of relatively small training datasets.

We conduct a rigorous re-examination of recent assertions claiming to observe Big Apple effects (BAEs)—defined as photon final states carrying greater energy than the incident nucleus via gamma-ray spectroscopy—within light nuclear reactions. Expressly concurring with prior observations, we assert that past data analysis did not provide sufficient statistical validation; however, our high-luminosity dataset analyzed here definitively confirms the absence of distinct anomalies at energies exceeding the peak Coulomb excitation curve, thereby ruling out BAEs. We further note that recent calculations purporting to observe Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) effects in the photon nuclear interaction are actually derived from theoretical models predicting suppressed Coulomb excitation, a hypothesis already disproven by experimental results. Consequently, we are unable to support the utilization of BAEs, should they exist, as evidence for modified nuclear forces in proximity to a hypothetical proton radius, nor can we validate reliance on this phenomenon for understanding the evolution of cosmic objects or the synthesis of heavy elements. Finally, we clarify a critical instrumental artifact affecting previous studies: since the system's baseline excitation curve peak is narrower than the measurement line width, re-centering and normalization procedures are demanding precise knowledge of the peak location, which current phenomenological data lacks.

Linking experimental observations with computational predictions is essential for characterizing the physical properties of materials beyond typical approximations, particularly those relying on approximate filtering. Using high magnetic fields to induce a transition into a Dirac state at finite doping represents a recent breakthrough. Driven by this finding, we provide a forecast based on joint theoretical modeling. Our predictions accurately align with existing experimental data and now outline pathways for further investigation on highly oriented diamond crystals, utilizing pulsed magnetic fields and in-situ doping resonators to explore the stability of the Dirac state and explore the associated anomalous Dirac-Hall effects.

Bimodal distributions, characterized by two distinct peaks, frequently appear in user research, such as in binary choice tasks where design alternatives are being evaluated. Analyzing these patterns enables researchers to draw more nuanced conclusions and deliver deeper insights than unimodal data alone. However, the standard normal approximation, which fits single-humped distributions well, fails to adequately capture the complexity of bimodal results. Consequently, there is a lack of appropriate statistical tools for summarizing such data. Addressing the research community's need, this paper introduces the concept of a "bimodal normal," defined by four parameters: mean and dispersion for each individual mode. Consequently, new formulas have been developed to calculate bimodal confidence intervals and test the statistical significance of ratios, with this section focusing specifically on the formula for the bimodal standard deviation.

Discriminating a potentially massive neutral lepton that mixes with its massless neutrino counterpart against a pure charged current decay is a key objective for future $K$-decays at CERN's upgraded NA62 experiment. Human speech acts as a highly effective medium for sharing information within social circles. Nevertheless, openly voiced statements often expose sensitive details, inadvertently jeopardizing personal or organizational privacy. Prior works have addressed private speech synthesis (PSS) against known auditory background noises; however, these solutions assume the user explicitly provides non-sensitive input to be merged with noise privacy. People often speak indirectly about sensitive topics by combining real content with distracting sound, expecting listeners to filter out the noise and identify the core message. To do so, some callers may choose to synthesize the noise themselves using varied voices or further manipulate its intensity and timbre to better mask their true intent. This paper introduces a human-centric approach for generating speech that people may use to protect sensitive voice data from eavesdroppers by letting them control the synthetic background audio directly with their speech inputs. Specifically, we introduce three main features that enhance privacy through flexible voice generation of distracting sound: (1) the ability for inputs to dictate the type of synthetic noise, (2) the ability for inputs to select the voice giving said noise so as not to give away the speaker identity associated with said noise, and (3) the ability for inputs to change the pitch and loudness of said noise. We introduce MaskedSpeech, which achieves the human-like pattern putting speech before noise while also maintaining high perceptual clarity of the spoken and noise components plus the underlying semantic relationship between them all, thus successfully hiding all sensitive voice data in there too.

This study utilizes an analytical stochastic model to examine the threshold dynamics of quantum error correction (QEC) protocols when executed on imperfect classical random graphs, focusing specifically on quantum codes derived from random sparse Gell-Mann structures. These Gell-Mann graphs differ significantly in topological complexity and sparsity when compared to their topologically identical quantum counterparts, allowing us to interpret QEC behavior through the lens of stochastic dynamics on simplified quantum analogs. Within our framework, we analyze the evolution from disordered graph configurations toward critical percolation phases and beyond, defining new concepts of percolation and correlation lengths that apply exclusively to quantum scenarios. These models serve to predict important metrics, including the current and future operating thresholds of these QEC circuits. Furthermore, we introduce the methodology of "quantumization" to transform stochastic realizations into corresponding quantum counterparts, effectively shifting problems involving complex quantum code dynamics to more manageable probabilistic models.

Topological quantum computing relies heavily on Topological Quantum Cometers (TQCs), a class of materials characterized by topological bulk gaps and metallic surfaces enriched with Dirac spinors. Currently, the search for TQCs focused on expanding the material platform while keeping the topological band gap large. The latter specification is essential for minimizing decoy effects and operational costs in quantum computing processes, as well as for stabilizing non-abelion anyons at room temperatures—a potential future target although not currently realized. Recent studies have identified 1D nanofibers of elemental Tellium as a source of large-gap TQCs; however, functionalizing this discovery with adjacent atomic layers of Tellium creates a binary layer structure susceptible to self-standing stabilization through recent advances in two-dimensional technology fabrication methods. Our research introduces a first-principles investigation into the physical and chemical properties of functionalized Tellium. We uncover that strain engineering or substituting adjacent atomic layers can induce various electronic behaviors within the binary layer system, including insulation, metallicity, and hole topology. Most notably, substitutional elasticity can result in the formation of surface states.

Developing new annotated resources for NLP is typically resource-intensive, particularly when establishing fresh languages or expanding multilingual tools. To alleviate this burden, researchers often reuse existing multi-lingual semantic frameworks, such as WordNet or BabelNet, which consist of manually constructed graphs of entities and their relationships. When adding relations to these multilingual knowledge bases to align with an input text corpus, the primary algorithm faced is typically a consistent representation model. Existing approaches, however, struggle to effectively leverage rich structural information from the knowledge base while remaining robust against noise within the corpus.

We propose a new algorithm designed specifically for representing members within multilingual shared semantic structures via knowledge base integration and text corpus features. The method uses three key representations: (1) the frequency with which an entity appears in surrounding context windows across corpus documents to capture its distribution; (2) the average frequency derived from all of that entity’s linked counterparts in the knowledge base to provide consistent baseline comparison; and (3) the vector difference between the knowledge base role-based embedding and corpus frequency embedding to encode how that object relates both globally and locally within both structures.

Empirical evaluations across three different knowledge bases and corpora demonstrate substantial improvements over prior methods, lowering training times and expenses when building multilingual semantic frameworks.

Active auditory localization involves an agent moving through a environment to determine its own location and that of sound sources. In this paper, we address a difficult scenario involving a 0.5-meter-tall agent navigating a wet, slippery floor while localizing both movable and stationary sounds in 3D space. We investigate how to successfully localize sound despite 2D slip-based motion and establish a 3D audio perception capability. To achieve a robust system, we developed an original, computationally efficient, depth-aware 2D audio filter that accurately maps probability maps of sound sources. By combining this with a standard potential fields approach, we created a localization strategy that avoids costly and computationally heavy 3D mappings. Experimental results confirm the localizer achieves high-precision audio spatial mapping. Additionally, our study reveals a physical robotics threshold: stable 3D audio localization in unstructured, real-world settings requires either complete free slip conditions or the implementation of specific anti-slip mechanisms on the robot.
